explanations.answer: No they devise injustice in their hearts
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. David doesn't dance around it. He says, "No, in your hearts you devise injustice; with your hands you mete out violence on the earth." (Psalm 58:2) The trouble starts inside and then shows up in what their hands do.

explanations.answer: Yes they judge the people fairly
explanations.explanation: I get why a baker might hope so, friend, because a ruler is supposed to be fair. But David's answer is the opposite. He says, "No, in your hearts you devise injustice…" (Psalm 58:2) His question wasn't a real question. It was a charge.

explanations.answer: He leaves the answer up to God
explanations.explanation: Good thought, but David doesn't wait. He answers his own question right away with a plain "No." (Psalm 58:2) He says they devise injustice in their hearts and mete out violence with their hands. He turns to God for help in verse 6, but the answer about the rulers comes first.

Not quite, friend. David says, "The wicked are estranged from the womb; the liars go astray from birth." (Psalm 58:3) He puts it at the very start, not after they grow up. That's a heavy way to say how deep it runs.

That's right, baker. David says, "The wicked are estranged from the womb; the liars go astray from birth." (Psalm 58:3) He puts the going astray at the very beginning, not later in life. He's painting how deep this goes.

Yes, baker. David says the cobra "shuts its ears, refusing to hear the tune of the charmer who skillfully weaves his spell." (Psalm 58:4-5) The charmer plays his best song and gets nothing. That's the picture of the rulers: they won't listen.
That's what a cobra does in the movies, friend, so I see the pull. But David's cobra does the opposite. It "shuts its ears" and refuses to hear the tune. (Psalm 58:4-5) No swaying at all.

A cobra with a grudge would make a fine story, but that's not what David writes. He says it "shuts its ears, refusing to hear the tune of the charmer." (Psalm 58:4-5) The picture is about a cobra that won't listen, not one that bites.

Hold on, friend, that's not where the prayer goes. David prays, "O God, shatter their teeth in their mouths; O LORD, tear out the fangs of the lions." (Psalm 58:6) He asks for the fangs to be torn out, not for the lions to lie down in peace.

That's right, baker. The prayer says, "O God, shatter their teeth in their mouths; O LORD, tear out the fangs of the lions." (Psalm 58:6) David asks for the fangs to be torn out. Nothing about lions lying down in peace.

Yes, baker. David prays, "May they vanish like water that runs off; when they draw the bow, may their arrows be blunted." (Psalm 58:7) A blunted arrow can't do its work. He's asking for their weapons to fail.
I think the bow threw you off, friend. David prays, "…when they draw the bow, may their arrows be blunted." (Psalm 58:7) So he does ask for it. Blunted arrows can't do their damage.

explanations.answer: That they never see the sun
explanations.explanation: Right, baker. David prays, "…may they never see the sun." (Psalm 58:8) This is a heavy part of the song, so I'll just say it plainly and not joke around. He's asking God to end the wicked's reach.

explanations.answer: That they live to see old age
explanations.explanation: That's a kind wish, friend, but it isn't in David's prayer. He asks, "…may they never see the sun." (Psalm 58:8) It's a heavy verse, and it goes the other direction from a long life.

explanations.answer: That they find their way home
explanations.explanation: A gentle answer, baker, but David's song is not gentle here. He prays, "…may they never see the sun." (Psalm 58:8) This is one of the heavy verses, and it says nothing about finding their way home.
That's it, baker. The psalm says, "Before your pots can feel the burning thorns—whether green or dry—He will sweep them away." (Psalm 58:9) It's fast. The pots never even get warm.

I think the patient dad in me liked that one, friend. But the psalm doesn't say it. It says, "…He will sweep them away." (Psalm 58:9) No extra warning in that verse, and it happens before the pots feel the thorns.

Hiding is a fair guess, baker, but the verse has no hiding spot. It says, "Before your pots can feel the burning thorns—whether green or dry—He will sweep them away." (Psalm 58:9) Swept away, and fast.

That's right, baker. David says, "The righteous will rejoice when they see they are avenged…" (Psalm 58:10) The song goes from the wicked to the righteous here. Their joy comes when they see they are avenged.

Not quite, friend. The text says, "The righteous will rejoice when they see they are avenged…" (Psalm 58:10) So David does say they will rejoice. The turn to the righteous is the hopeful part of the song.
Yes, baker. "Then men will say, 'There is surely a reward for the righteous!'" (Psalm 58:11) After all that heavy stuff, the song lands on hope for the righteous.

A warning fits the rest of the song, friend, I'll give you that. But the line says, "There is surely a reward for the righteous!" (Psalm 58:11) The warning part was for the rulers, and this verse turns to the righteous.
After a psalm this intense, I can see why that one tempted you, baker. But the verse says, "There is surely a reward for the righteous!" (Psalm 58:11) A reward, not a burden. It's a hopeful ending.

That's right, baker. The people say, "There is surely a God who judges the earth!" (Psalm 58:11) David opened by asking if the rulers judge uprightly. He closes by pointing to the God who judges the earth.
The righteous are the ones who rejoice, friend, but they're not the judge. The people say, "There is surely a God who judges the earth!" (Psalm 58:11) The judging belongs to God.
A new king would be a tidy fix, baker, but the psalm never says one. The people say, "There is surely a God who judges the earth!" (Psalm 58:11) The one who judges is God Himself.
